I fully endorse this petition for the following reasons:

1. The Origins of Arbitration

Initially, arbitration was formulated for parties with comparable negotiating strength [1(p. 1631)] [2(p. 65)] and for sectors seldom addressed by the judiciary [3(p. 1)]. It wasn't devised for disagreements between consumers and banks. A Senator once expressed anxiety about arbitration contracts potentially being imposed on trapped customers or workers. Assurances were provided by the bill's proponents that such scenarios were not their intention [1(p. 1636) via citation] [4(p. 644)].

2. The Unequal Nature of Arbitration

Although contemporary Supreme Court verdicts deem certain terms lawful, it doesn't necessarily mean they're equitable. Records show that consumers are less successful in arbitration compared to court settings, mainly because of the diminished procedural and substantive rights arbitration offers.

Post-arbitration decisions, the avenue for an appeal is almost non-existent. Moreover, arbitrators aren't bound by legal statutes [5]. Notably, under New York's jurisdiction, blatant disregard for the law isn't a valid ground to overturn an arbitration decision [6(p. 995)].

Arbitration might not offer the comprehensive discovery that courts grant [4(p. 638)]. These contracts can eliminate punitive damages, abbreviate the statute of limitations, or introduce other procedural constraints. Companies exploit this feature. A disparity in information ensures that injustices can persist under the banner of "expediency." Often, consumers don't possess the comprehensive information that corporations have.

3. The Illusion of Arbitration Choice

In most scenarios, consumers feel compelled to agree to a company's imposed arbitration clause. On the infrequent occasion that a consumer comprehends the stipulated arbitration condition, their option is usually to concur. Competing firms often have similar mandates. Identifying a non-arbitration enforcing competitor would be a time-intensive task for a consumer [1(p. 1632)]. Opt-out provisions, when present, are notoriously challenging to enact.

Such clauses are typically concealed in intricate legal jargon, often accentuated with ALL-CAPS typography, making comprehension difficult [7].

The variations across financial institutions make it impractical for mandatory arbitration to truly serve consumers. When probed about significant factors, consumers rarely mentioned dispute resolution mechanisms. When shown a list of credit card features, they ranked dispute resolution last [8(p. 106)]. This isn't indicative of consumer apathy. While they deeply value their rights, they might lack the nuanced understanding of pre-emptive measures. Notably, 38.6% of survey participants under arbitration clauses believed they retained the right to litigation [8(p. 106)].

4. The Misconception of Arbitration Efficiency

A prevailing misconception is that arbitration is swift and streamlined. In reality, it is the opposite. The arbitration procedure largely caters to the whims of the agreement's drafter. Defendants that resist cooperation aren't uncommon, leveraging arbitration's structure for postponements [9] [10]. Some corporations have embedded obligatory prolonged mediation phases or capped simultaneous arbitrations, causing extensive delays. Added to this, confidentiality clauses might hinder consumers from recognizing potential infringements.ached file(s).

I support the Petition in its entirety.

1. History of Arbitration

Arbitration was designed for entities of equal bargaining power. [1(p. 1631)] [2(p. 65)] and for industries whose needs are not typically handled by the legal system. [3(p. 1)]. It was never intended for disputes between consumers and financial institutions. In fact when one Senator voiced a concern that arbitration contracts might be "offered on a take-it-or-leave-it basis to captive customers or employees," the Senator was reassured by the bill's supporters that they did not intend for the bill to cover such situations. [1(p. 1636) via citation] [4(p. 644)]

2. Arbitration is Inherently Unfair

While recent supreme court decisions have made terms legal, they have not made them fair.
It is well established that consumers are more likely to lose in arbitration than in Court. This is due to the lack of procedural and substantive rights that come with arbitration.

Once the arbitrator has ruled, there is no realistic possibility for appeal. In fact, arbitrators are not even required to follow the law. [5] In fact, under New York law, manifest disregard for the law is not an eligible reason to vacate an arbitration judgement. [6(p. 995)]

Arbitration may not provide parties with the same extent of discovery that a court would.[4(p. 638)] The contracts preclude punitive damages, shorten statute of limitations, or insert additional procedural limitations. This is a feature that companies rely on. Information asymmetry allows for injustices to prevail under the guise of "efficiency". It is rare that consumers have access to the same set of data that companies do.

3. Arbitration is Not a Choice

The practical reality is that consumers have little if any choice but to accept the arbitration provision mandated by the company. Even in those rare instances when a consumer has read and understood the arbitration clause being required by the company, she likely has little choice but to accept the clause. In many instances competitor companies will require the same or a similar clause. Even if a competitor existed that did not mandate arbitration, it likely would not be worth the consumer's time to conduct the extensive research necessary to identify the competitor.[1(p. 1632)] Even if opt-out clauses exist, they are arbitrarily painful to effect.

Arbitration clauses are buried in fine print. The clauses are often printed in ALL‐CAPS text which is harder to read. [7]

There are too many differences amongst financial institutions for pre-dispute mandatory arbitration to be meaningful. In fact when asked about relevant factors no consumers volunteered an answer that even implicitly referenced dispute resolution procedures and when presented with a list of nine features of credit cards consumers identified dispute resolution procedures as being relevant less often than any of the other eight options.[8(p. 106)] This is not an argument that consumers don't care. Consumers care very much when their rights are violated. They may just not be sophisticated enough to be aware of the actions they have to take in advance. Over a third (38.6%) of respondents whose agreements include pre-dispute arbitration clauses believed they could sue in court. [8(p. 106)]

4. Arbitration is neither speedy nor efficient

One of the arguments in favor of arbitration is that such proceedings are more efficient. It is anything but. Arbitration proceeds according to the whims of the entity that wrote the agreement. Recalcitrant defendants are common and use the nature of arbitration to delay trial. [9] [10] For instance some companies have inserted mandatory elongated "mediation" sessions or added restrictions on the number of in flight arbitrations. This can delay cases for years. Companies also insert confidentiality clauses which may restrict the ability for consumers to even know they've been harmed.

I strongly support this petition, and highly encourage the CFPB to promulgate rulemaking reflecting the petition.  I am a consumer protection attorney and almost exclusively represent consumers who were ripped off by buy-here, pay-here (BHPH) car dealerships in Florida.  I have had dozens of cases that I have turned away because of the onerous arbitration provisions and I could not promise the potential clients that they would receive a fair shake in arbitration.  My personal experience with arbitration is that it is highly variable and dependent on the specific arbitrator.  Arbitration has certainly not been cheaper and has not been quicker than most of the cases I have litigated in court against BHPH dealers.  I have taken several depositions of car dealers where I have asked about the arbitration provisions.  Not one of them had an accurate understanding of what arbitration was, how it works, or how much it costs.  They certainly never discussed it with their customers (my clients), so it was not something they negotiated.  It was only offered on a take-it-or-leave it basis.  In all or virtually all cases, the arbitration agreement was never even presented to the customer until they had already signed the buyer's order and/or retail installment sales contract; this means they were already bound to the contract by the time arbitration was even mentioned.  In some cases, my clients had already paid the down payment to the dealer before they were given the arbitration agreement and told to sign it.  Some of the agreements also include other "alternative dispute mechanism" requirements, such as mediation, that can cost my clients over $1,000.  Then, I have had car dealers who demanded arbitration after I filed a lawsuit, but who refused to pay the high filing fees associated with arbitration, causing significant delays and additional expense to my clients.  Simply put, my experience shows that BHPH dealers use the arbitration provision to try to discourage or coerce customers into giving up meritorious claims.  My experience also shows that arbitration is a very poor substitute for litigating cases in open court.  I highly encourage the CFPB to grant this petition and initiate appropriate rulemaking dealing with arbitration provisions forced upon consumers by BHPH dealerships.  Thank you.

Please stop allowing corporations to require people to sign or opt-out of arbitration clauses to access their services. We have a judicial system that works. Arbitration is wildly unfair and antithetical to our justice system. Corporations are literally invented to protect businesses. They already have the corporate shield they need. This massive cropping up of arbitration clauses everywhere (even on banks that are federally insured and should be "safe" for consumers) is such a massive overreach. These are not arms-length deals and in this so complex corporate world, no one has time to be opting out of arbitration clauses, sometimes by certified mail, left and right. It's ridiculous. I at least have been a consumer fraud attorney and know how massively unfair these arbitration clauses are in real life and what people are being forced to waive, but most people do not. The very basic Bill of Rights and the Constitution go over and over again that due process, right to a jury trial by our peers, etc., are all fundamental, bedrock principles in our legal system. If these massive corporations can just force everyone out of these foundational rights, what kind of a country are we then? This takes away both the duty of corporations to perform per their contract (as there is no real chance of enforcement) and takes away consumer rights to basic fundamental principles of our legal system. It's just wrong. It needs to stop. It is so wildly unfair. Please stop this. Even if no one ever files a suit against a corporation, they shouldn't be forced to waive the right to sue before they even know what legal problems they will have down the road with the corporation. And there certainly is no additional consideration for that term coming back to the consumer for that waiver. Thank you.

I support this measure.

The Katharine & George Alexander Community Law Center (‘Law Center’) is a clinical program for Santa Clara Law. The Law Center recently had a client that was adversely affected by a Buy Here Pay Here dealer’s arbitration clause in a vehicle purchase contract. The dealer in question, the Signature Motors (TSM) is exactly the kind of dealer that the California legislature had in mind when they enacted laws in 2012 requiring such dealers to disclose the fair market value of their vehicles and to offer 30-day warranties. Specifically, TSM sells older high-mileage cars that are drastically overpriced. After 2012 TSM wanted to continue selling drastically overpriced high-mileage used cars without disclosing their fair market value and without offering 30 day warranties. In 2018, the owner incorporated a ‘separate’ finance company – America One Credit Acceptance, LLC (AOCA) – for the sole purpose of evading California’s Buy Here Pay Here laws. AOCA is not – in any practical sense – separate from the dealership, it is owned and operated by the same individual at the same address as TSM.

The California legislature foresaw such a scheme. In order to be exempt from Buy Here Pay Here laws, a dealer must assign its credit contracts to lenders which are ‘unaffiliated’.

In 2020, during the height of the pandemic, TSM sold our client a 2011 Nissan Armada with over 170,000 miles. TSM sold the vehicle for $19,899 and did not disclose the reasonable market value of the vehicle. In fact, the market value of the vehicle was substantially less than the $19,899 purchase price. TSM offered no warranty on the vehicle which did, in fact, have mechanical problems. Shortly after our client requested that TSM repair the vehicle, TSM repossessed it. Our client, a sole proprietor of a small business, had his tools in the vehicle when it was repossessed. TSM never notified him how to regain the vehicle or his tools and our client became homeless due to the repossession. The Law Center first obtained photographic proof showing that the dealer was not offering warranties or disclosing values on any of its vehicles. The Law Center then filed suit not only to recover damages and restitution, but also as a private attorney general, to obtain a public injunction to bring TSM into compliance with California Buy Here Pay Here laws.

TSM hired counsel who contacted the Law Center. TSM’s counsel informed the Law Center that unless the client agreed to arbitrate the claim with AAA, TSM would file a motion to compel arbitration and would seek attorneys’ fees and costs associated with the motion. After stipulating to AAA arbitration, the client ultimately agreed to settle the case without obtaining any injunctive relief. The client was justifiably concerned about AAA’s willingness and ability to provide for injunctive relief. In this case, the dealer was able to use the arbitration process to avoid an injunction he would certainly have obtained if the case were allowed to proceed in court.

This case is in many way emblematic of the ways forced arbitration undermines consumer protections.

THIS IS LONG OVERDUE!  Corporations have been using forced arbitration to cheat their workers and customers for decades.  Ever since the U.S. Supreme Court's extreme, judicial activist expansion of the Federal Arbitration Act--a law passed nearly a hundred years ago, which was intended solely to affect federal court procedures--into every aspect of commercial life, it has creeped into nearly every aspect of our daily lives.  Want internet?  A bank account?  A credit card?  To buy a car?  Arbitration.  It wouldn't be so bad if arbitration was actually a fair and impartial process that preserved your rights.  But for bizarre reasons that make no sense whatsoever, the Supreme Court has declared that arbitration agreements give corporations special powers (over and above normal contracts) to ban class actions, local court proceedings, and jury trials.  You can't even appeal a bad decision.  There is no public record of cases from which new case law can be created, so the law in many areas has been frozen since the mid 1990s.  And the only justification for it is corporate profits.  You should have fixed this long ago.  The Dodd-Frank bill gave you the authority to ban these abusive contractual provisions in consumer finance, and it is time to do so.  Now.
There should be a rule as to the font size of the printing in any agreement, like a loan, a rental agreement, etc.  The minimum should be 10 points, at least.
I write to urge you to preserve our 7th Amendment right to a jury trial and stop forced arbitration.

I am a consumer rights attorney. I write in support of the petition. I wish to provide this additional example of an abusive arbitration clause, inserted in Wells Fargo Bank's Deposit Account Agreement, which is presumably imposed on the millions of bank customers nationwide. At page 35 of the 40-page "agreement," you will find the following language:  "Arbitration is beneficial because it provides a legally binding decision in a more streamlined, cost-effective manner than a typical court case. But, the benefit of arbitration is diminished if either Wells Fargo or you refuse to submit to arbitration following a lawful demand. Thus, the party that does not agree to submit to arbitration after a lawful demand must pay all of the other party’s costs and expenses for compelling arbitration." This fee-shifting provision is unconscionable, rendering it virtually impossible for consumers to challenge arbitration, unless their attorney is willing to absorb this substantial financial risk. It is also in direct conflict with the Consumer Rules of both AAA and JAMS, which require businesses to pay all costs beyond a small filing fee that the consumer must pay. I have attached a copy of the "agreement."

From: Ed Mierzwinski <edm@pirg.org>
Date: Tue, Nov 14, 2023 at 8:32 AM
Subject: RE: Docket ID CFPB-2023-0047, Petition for Rulemaking



14 November 2023
Director Rohit Chopra
Consumer Financial Protection Bureau
1700 G Street NW
Washington, DC 20552

Submitted via regulations.gov

RE: Docket ID CFPB-2023-0047, Petition for Rulemaking: To Require Meaningful Consumer Consent Regarding the Use of Arbitration to Resolve Disputes Involving Consumer Financial Products and Services

Dear Director Chopra:

RE: Docket ID CFPB-2023-0047, Petition for Rulemaking: To Require Meaningful Consumer Consent Regarding the Use of Arbitration to Resolve Disputes Involving Consumer Financial Products and Services

U.S. PIRG submits these brief comments in support of the Petition for Rulemaking, To Require Meaningful Consumer Consent Regarding the Use of Arbitration to Resolve Disputes Involving Consumer Financial Products and Services, which appeared on the Rulemaking Docket on September 14, 2023.

As an organization dedicated to consumer protection, we strongly support the petition filed to require meaningful consumer consent to arbitration, and to end the sordid and unseemly practice of forced arbitration.

As you may know, we have supported the CFPB since before its creation. And after over twelve years of its successes for aggrieved consumers, it is clear that the idea of the CFPB needs no defense; it only needs more defenders.

But without a tough rule regulating high cost lending, it cannot prevent all consumer abuses.

The most important thing you must do is ban pre-dispute arbitration. The courts have somewhat naively left this door open and it must be closed. Shut tight.

Forced arbitration certainly harms young consumers--who are just starting their financial lives. As you know, the PIRGs were founded by and still place a strong emphasis on teaching and protecting young consumers. We are pleased that the CFPB shares our concern for students and other young people.

But all consumers face the threat of of harm or being hurt or defrauded by forced arbitration clauses, often hidden in the small print or what is often called "mice type."



It's quite pathetic that corporate wrongdoers still hide behind these clauses; why can't they do things in the light of day?



The CFPB can end this unfair practice and help consumers a lot with this simple rule.

Again, The courts have unwisely left this door open and it must be closed. Please shut it tight, once and for all.



Sincerely,



Edmund Mierzwinski

Senior Director, Federal Consumer Programs,

U.S PIRG
